THE THOMAS HERESY CASE.
CHICAGO, Aug. 26.—Dr. Willings has appointed the Rev. J. C. Steoughton, of Aurora, to assist Drs. Hatfield and Jewett in the prosecution of the case of the Rev. Dr. Thomas who is charged with heresy.

AN ABANDONED WOMAN KILLED.
St. PAUL, Minn., Aug. 26.—Kate Hutton, a notorious woman, was shot fatally about midnight by "Ed" Wright, her negro paramour, with whom she was living on the prairie north of the city. Wright claims that the shooting was accidental.

POISONING HIS ENTIRE FAMILY.
WAUKESHA, Wis., Aug. 26.—One Howard, living in Delafield, ten miles north of this place, poisoned his entire family yesterday, and his wife and two children have died. An ungovernable temper and domestic troubles are the causes assigned for the deed.

INDIANA CROP PROSPECTS.
INDIANAPOLIS, Ind., Aug. 26.—W. H. Ragan, president of the State Board of Agriculture, says that the crops in the central and southern portions of the State will not be one-half the average, but in the northern part there will be about a two-thirds crop. All the cereals are suffering in a like degree, and if there is not a heavy rain in a very few days in many counties of the State nearly all the corn will be cut up for fodder. The wheat prospect is bad, and there is very little hay. Fruit, especially apples, promised well, but in the last few weeks the drought has had a telling effect upon them, and they will fall below the average.

Tar, Feathers and Murder.
DETROIT, Mich., August 27.—A negro, named Charles Dow, was murdered on Tuesday last in the township of Riley, Clinton county. The negro had many enemies, although not of a quarrelsome disposition. It was generally believed in the neighborhood, however, that he abused his wife and was cruel to his stock, and abut a month ago a party of men broke into his house in the middle of the right, bound, gaged, tarred and feathered him, and threatened to take his life if he did not change his course. On the night in question his wife was absent. His house was again visited on Tuesday night, but by whom is not known. His body was found the next morning hanging in the barn, with a cut over the left eye, penetrating the skull, and sufficient to have caused instant death. There was also a cut on the back port of his head. One leg was dislocated and his back was badly bruised, indicating a terrible struggle. The body was covered with blood.

A dispatch from Brackett, Texas, dated the 26th inst., says: "While four horse thieves, belonging to an extensive gang which have been operating along the Rio Grande for a long time, were being brought to this place yesterday in charge of officers, they were attacked near the town of Dolores, and all the thieves killed."

At Forest City, Ark., on the night of the 27th inst., Lute Wallace invited S. C. Apperson, city marshal, to take a cigar, and while standing at the corner of the saloon Apperson drew a revolver and said: "I think I will shoot you." Wallace, thinking he was jesting, replied, "Shoot away." Apperson was killed for the murder, for the two men were apparently on the murder, the best of terms.

In a street brawl at Silverton, Col., on the 27th., D. G. Ogsbury was killed by roughs.

Charles Dew, a negro, was murdered at his house in Riley township, Clinton county, Mich., on the night of the 23d inst. He was quarrelsome and had abused his wife. Several days ago unknown men men tarred and feathered him.

While James Boyd, of Owensville, Ky., was watching at the bedside of his sick sister, Mrs. McClure, some unknown person person through the window at Boyd. The shock caused Mrs. McClure's death.

A man named Holt was killed at Washington Springs, Chickasaw Nation, on the 26th inst. A dispute over a game of cards.

A gang of desperadoes who had been committing lawless acts in Dangerfield, Titus, Hopkins, Hunt and Trayson, Texas, were pursued by citizens who succeeded in killing one of the outlaws.

Ben Blanton, ex-sheriff of Cook County, had a difficulty with a man named James Todd, who had been a witness against him, and each vowed wengeance on the other. The men met and began shooting at once and both were instantly killed.

John Hermann, a livery stable keeper, and formerly city marshal of Deshler, O., was shot and instantly killed by Peter Cole, a drayman. The killing is the result of a long-standing feud between these two men.

Unknown parties entered the jail at Monroe, La., on the morning of the 23d inst., and secured Perry Mason and Alex. Wilson, (colored) charged with murder, and hanged them.

A tragedy occurred about ten miles from Edgefield County, S. C., on the 24th inst., between J. W. Buzzard and his son and J. W. Timmerman, in which Timmerman was killed and Buzzard and his son seriously injured. An old feud was the cause of the affair. The weapons used were double-barreled shot-guns.

An unknown assassin killed Alderian Pitts, a wealthy and highly respected farmer of Rutherford County, Penn., on the 22d inst. It is thought the cause of the killing originated from a divorce suit instituted some time since between Pitts and his wife.

A teamster named House and Cal Hatcher, a hackman, had a quarrel at Kansas City, Mo., on the 22d inst., about temporary shed room occupied by teams, and House shot Hatcher through the abdomen. House escaped and is still at large. Hatcher will die.

Two desperadoes named Folsom and Hobbs, having lost money in a gambling place at Waldron, Scott county, Texas, returned to the place the following night and shot John Stewart the keeper of the place. Billy Messingale who was visiting the Stewart family received a ball through the head, and will die.

Orange, Texas, is in a ferment, owing to recent lawless acts, and the citizens have thus far hanged six miscreants—Bob and Sam Saxon and four negroes. At last accounts Charles Delno was about to be tried by a "Kangaroo" court of lynchers and the county is being secured by regulators.

MICHIGAN.

Jaaper Cross, an old jeweler at Adrian has failed. Liabilities $15,000. Assets $9,000.

John Berry of Battle Creek, was accidentally shot and killed at Armenia, N. Y.

James Howes of Battle Creek, was killed at Muskegon while coupling care.

Mrs. McKane was seriously injured at Flint by being thrown from a carriage, the horse becoming frightened at a passing elephant.

Percy, a six years old son of Richard Emmons of Cassopolis, fell from a load of lumber, and one of the wheels passed over his breast, killing him instantly.

Base Ball—Chicago 8, Detroit 6. Twelve innings.

Michael Firnane, County Prosecuting Attorney, and ex-President of the Detroit board of education, died at Minneapolis, aged 30.

Fifty of the Chinese students recalled by the government passed through Detroit on the 23rd, on their way home.

Postmaster Vincent of Lapeer, had his farm, barn and contents burned by tramps. Loss $3,000. No insurance.

Jas. G. Wright of Albion is dead, age 60.

Henry McCormick held at East Sagliuw for a Canadian murder in 1870 is to be extradited.

A man giving his name as Albert Smith hired a horse and buggy from Tiffany, a Dundee livery man, and was arrested at Monroe the following day after having sold the rig for $49.

George C. Collins, once a prominent business man in Ypsilanti, has just died at the county house. He was sent there some four months since, his complaint being softening of the brain caused by drink.

W. P. Andrus, state senator from Kent county in 1877 was being taken to the insane asylum at Kalamazoo, when he escaped near Battle Creek and at last reports had not yet been heard from.

A new house just built by Alphonso Hutchins on his farm near Battle Creek has been destroyed by fire with all its contents. The fire is supposed to have been set by a tramp. The loss is $4,000, with an insurance of $1,200 in the Farmers' mutual.

A collision on the D. L. & N. R. R. near Portland wrecked two freight trains and delayed travel several hours.

Jacob Ranswiler, a German about 50 years of age, committed suicide at Albion by taking Paris green. He was intemperate.

Base ball—Detroit 7, Chicago 5.

Chas. Dew, a negro, living in the township of Riley, was murdered by blows upon the head with some sharp instrument and afterwards hanged in his own barn, the whole being apparently done in cold blood. Dew was a small man and not of a fighting disposition, but he had many enemies. It was charged that he abused his wife and was cruel to his stock, and about three weeks ago a party of men forced his door one night, took him out and bound, gagged and "arred and feathered him, and threatened his life if he did not change his course. E. O. Shaw, of the Newaygo Republican and postmaster of the place, took poison with suicidal intent. He had been absent for a week or more in Chicago, and as supposed, had been indulging quite freely. He is expected to recover.

A young man named Alexander Cofferen of Elk township, was lost off the steamer M. D. Ward at Marine City last night with a brother. They lay down on the deck aft to go to sleep and in the morning were missing. A woman on the boat reports having heard a noise and seen an object in the water while the boat was at the dock a. Dr. Malcolm Mc. Vicar, for the past year principal of the state normal school at Ypsilanti, has accepted the professorship of New Testament interpretation in Toronto university, made vacant by the death of the Rev. John Torrance.

A 6-year-old son of Oliver Shampine fell into a vat of hot brine at Winsor & Co.'s salt block, Post Auston, and died the next day.

Monroe county veterans to the number of 300 attended the reunion at Monroe.

Messrs. Westbrook Divine and Thomas F. Moore, of the board of managers of the state house of correction at Ionia, failing to resign their offices in response to a suggestion of the governor, were yesterday peremptorily removed by him. Joseph T. Escott of Big Rapids, Abraham H. Piper of Lapeer, and George W. Buckingham of Flint were appointed as a new board, their duties to commence August 31.

There is a general strike of saw mill men at Oscoda, in this state, and all the mills are stopped. The strikers interfered with men wishing to work, and an attempt by Sheriff King with three deputies to arrest some of the offenders caused a riot in which the sheriff shot one man in the hip. At last accounts there were 700 men parading the streets, with great excitement and fear of further collisions. The men struck for a reduction of time to 11 hours.

A. M. Flint and Andrew Hardy of Nashville, have been bound over for trial on a charge of bribery by Justice Greenfield at Hastings.

Mrs. James Geer of Lapeer fell forward in her chair and instantly expired. Heart disease.

Miss J. A. King, for the past ten years superintendent of public schools at Charlotte, has accepted the chair of history in the state normal school Ypsilanti.

As Peter P. Greiner of Mt. Clements, and a party of his friends were returning from an excursion to Lake St. Clair, his son Bertie, a lad 7 years old, while playing about the bow of the boat, fell overboard and was drowned. The body has been recovered.

The contract for the erection of the new school house at Portland has been awarded to J. H. Hoskine of Grand Rapids for $9,877.

Four boys who were arrested for breaking into a Chicago and Grand Trunk freight car at Port Huron have escaped. Two of them got out of the city jail one night, and the remaining two took their departure the following night.

The vehicle is built and furnished with all the needful appliances, including medicines, stimulants, mattress, bandages, plaster etc. It will be manned by a skillful attendant and a driver, and will be continuously on duty within telephonic call by the police or any other citizen.

Enemata have been again resorted to and they are highly stimulated and frequently administered. It is hoped by this to arrest the continued sleepiness that is considered an undesirable symptom. The inflamed gland is discharging through the left ear. The most serious results are anticipated, though all hope is not abandoned by the attending physicians.

The "Western Michigan Farmers Club" organized at Grand Rapids.

NEWS OF THE WEEK.
MICHIGAN.
The body of Ex-alderman Schultz of Detroit was found in the river. He had been missing for several days.

The Swedish church at Muskegon and its contents, valued at $1,500 was entirely destroyed by fire. It was partially insured.

Daniel Everett of Girard township, had his barn and sheds, with all their contents, burned loss about $1,500; insured for $1,000.

Jos. Kunderhlot, aged 18, a butcher living at Jackson was drowned in Round lake by the capsizing of a boat.

John O. Seffron an old actor, died at the Franklin House Detroit.

Stephen Chalfield, an intemperate painter of Albion, suicided by taking laudanum.

The house, barn and contents belonging to Lan West, at Orion, caught from a marsh which was fired by a passing engine and was burned. Loss, $1,200; insurance, $500.

Mrs. Tyrrell, an old resident of Kalamazoo, died at that place aged 92 years.

Burglaries broke into the safe of C. S. Crandali's grocery store at Harbor Springs and escaped with about $400.

While a steam-thresher was running on the farm of John Welch of Sunfield, sparks set fire to a straw stack, which burned, together with a barn and contents, and adjoining buildings. Loss, $1,200; insured in the Continental. The woods near by caught fire, and it was with great difficulty that a general conflagration was prevented.

John Berry, formerly of Brockway Center, St. Clair county, was found dead in the woods near one of Ward's camps, and was brought down to Ludington for interment.

Reed City is to have water works.

The board of officers appointed to select the companies of state troops to go to Yorktown, have designated the following: 1st regiment Co. A., Ann Arbor; Co. B., Adrian; 2nd regiment, Co. B., Grand Rapids; Co. G., Ionia; 3rd regiment, Co. D., Bay City; Co. E., East Saginaw.

The forest fires now raging in the eastern part of the state nearly equal those of 10 years ago, and in some places are reported as even worse. There has been a frightful loss of life, just how large cannot be told. A number of horrible deaths are reported at Richmondville, including those of three persons roasted alive in a well. The total number of deaths thus far reported is about 20, and it seems likely that the end is not yet. A woman in Sanilac county locked her two children in the house to go for help against the approaching fire, and returned to find that the house had burned and her children had perished in it. A great many people are fleeing to the lake shore to save their lives. The fires appear worst in Saginaw, Tuscola and Sanilac counties, but are breaking out at many points. Several villages are burned and many others threatened. The fires sweep over farms so as to kill even the pigs and chickens, and a great many families are left entirely destitute and must be aided at once.

J B. Wright & Co.'s planing mill at Port Huron has been burned together with a large amount of dressed lumber. Loss $20,000. Insurance $3,000.

John D. Bennett of Palmer Station, was committed at Hastings in default of bail, on a charge of obtaining goods under false pretenses.

Hon. John M. Harris, Judge of the Probate Court, Grand Rapids, is sued for breach of promise by Miss Hattie Holcourt. Damages claimed $10,000.

The new state asylum is to be located with special reference to the requirements of a distinct northern district.

Samuel Massey's saw and shingle mill, located one mile south of McBrides, was burned. Loss $3,000; insurance $2,000.

It is impossible to at present define the extent of the destruction of life and property by the forest fires. Huron and Sanilac counties may be said to be devastated. Reports are contradictory and unsatisfactory, communication being in many instances completely cut off. A great loss of life has certainly occured. Probably 200 is much below the aggregate. The tales of suffering and death are harrowing in the extreme.

The Michigan forest fires prove to be in destruction of life and properly the greatest calamity of the year. The lives lost are estimated at 200 at the lowest, and reports indicate that the figure is likely to be considerably higher. The great disaster was confined almost exclusively to Sanilac and Huron counties. One man traveling about the burnt district is said to have seen the bodies of 116 persons killed by the fire. Forty-five bodies have been found in a single village. The towns back from the shore in Sanilac and Huron counties, from which little has before been heard, are found to have suffered terribly, although no detailed reports are yet given. Through great districts the destruction is complete, and the fire is ended. The sufferings among those who escaped with their lives is severe and widespread, and urgent calls for aid are heard upon every hand. Hundreds and thousands of people, many of these but yesterday well-to-do, are flocking into villages entirely destitute and fairly naked and hungry. In the Saginaw Valley the fires are suiciding, and in some localities rains have ended all danger.

Hulbert Hall of Clio is held for an assault with intent to kill John Z. Richards whom he dangerously injured.

F. D. Lacey's shingle mill at Nirvana was entirely destroyed by fire. Loss $2,500; no insurance.

Base ball—Detroit 6, Cleveland 4.

As later reports come in the worst fears in regard to the Michigan fires are realized. A great tract in Sanliac and Huron counties, 100 miles long on the shore and 20 to 60 miles deep, is mostly burned over, involving a loss of life estimated at from 300 to 1,000, and of property to the extent of millions. Many of the details are almost too horrible for belief. The call for help grows more and more urgent, and already a great many thousand dollars are subscribed, and the whole country is becoming aroused to the work.

The body of Thos. Green, who disappeared from Coldwater, about three months since, has been found hanging to a tree in the outskirts of that city.

Mrs. Galen Johnson was scalded at Fenton by the bursting of a can of tomatoes that she was putting up.

There are 12 girls at the reform school for girls at Adrian.

Robertson Culbertson, a pioneer of Lenawee county, died at Clinton September 2. He came to Tecumseh from Groveland, N. Y., 45 years ago.

The relatives of Mrs. Caroline Lusk assembled on Sept. 1 at the residence of Samuel Sudborough, two miles northeast of Adrian, to celebrate Mrs. Lusk's 90th birthday. Four generations were present to do her honor.

The Macomb county court-house is nearly completed and will cost some $30,000. It is said that the contractor will be out of pocket some $3,000.

The parties who tarred and feathered Dew, the colored man who was murdered in Biley, Clinton county, a few weeks ago, have been discovered. A. W. Burrett confesses to being a party to the crime, and implicates seven others besides himself. The murder is still abroad.

The police have received an offer of $250 reward from the Underwriters of New York for the apprehension of the Thomasville incendiaries.

A correspondent calls the attention of the Post-Appal to the number of blind and cripple beggars on the streets of Atlanta.

This communication between the authorities should be mutually kept up, and every Georgian should have a pride in advancing this great State institution."

There are at least two thousand farmers in Anderson county who have given liens this year to secure advances with which to make their crop, and if the law is repealed this winter what will they do next year? It is fair to presume that only those who cannot obtain supplies without liens give them, and why any one should desire to deprive them of its friendly aid is more than we can understand.

Public opinion in this county, as in every other section of the State, is divided on the question of the lien law, but we do not believe the clamorings for its repeal are so general as elsewhere. We believe the repealing of the law at the next session of the Legislature, on the heels of the general failure of the crops, would be a calamity from which the State would not recover for years to come. Let the law stand as it is. It is a necessity to the agricultural interests of the whole State. What would become of the thousands of poor farmers, both white and colored, who now obtain their advances under its provisions?

Mr. E. F. Stokes, counsel for Dodson, Burton, Adams and Bates, the Greenville incendiaries sentenced to be hanged on the 9th of September, has filed the necessary papers for an appeal with the Clerk of the Supreme Court. This would operate to stay the execution, but Mr. Stokes will probably obtain an order restraining the Sheriff from executing the sentence of the Court from one of the Justices. The Supreme Court will not meet until November, and even if the new trial asked for is not granted, the prisoners will have to be re-sentenced. They will therefore not be hanged before December at the earliest.

Hon. W. D. Johnson, of Marion, who is at present a member of the State Board of Agriculture, and was one of the delegates from this State to the Georgia Agricultural Society meeting in Rome, on his return home paid Hon. B. F. Crayton a visit of several days, during which quite a number of our citizens had the pleasure of meeting him in Anderson for the first time since the inquiries of reconstruction took him off of the Bench as one of our Chancellors of the old Court of Equity. The Chancellor is now practicing law, and is extensively engaged in agriculture. He is one of the most valuable members of the Board of Agriculture, and with a most genial and cultivated, though unassuming, gentleman. We were pleased to see him in our midst, and are gratified to learn that he carried with him favorable impressions of our county and its progress.

hardin-brothers-fredonia-1881-08-07.A23: New York Tribune: Mob are always cowardly. hardin-brothers-fredonia-1881-08-07.A29:
WESTERN LAWLESSNESS.
Lynching is now so common that it seldom excites general comment; but the lynching of lynchers is not so frequent. The Kansas affair, in which forty masked men overpowered the guards of Fredonia jail, but were put to flight by a pistol handed to one of the prisoners by a guard, with which he shot the leader, shows the folly of lynch law. Hero was a respected, well-to-do farmer killed while breaking the law, in order to expedite justice. Had the two murderers sought by the mob been at large, and had the people, pursuing them, indignant at the sluggishness or connivance of the law, killed them on sight, the affair would have been different; had the jail been thought insecure, and had it therefore been surrounded by a volunteer guard, that also would be intelligible; but the blind fury which wreaks popular vengeance on culprits caught, caged, and awaiting conviction under process of law, needs some such incident as that of Fredonia to expose its senselessless. The mob were really about to commit murder—however the provocation may have seemed to them to justify their act. In addition, they sought to break down the law, and they put its guardians into the dilemma of having to call on jail culprits to help them against the community.

t-noakes-oroville-1881-08-07.A13:
THE OROVILLE LYNCHING.
A mob took Thomas Noakes out of jail at Oroville, and hanged him. Noakes had murdered an inoffensive cripple by beating him, and it was undoubtedly a very aggravated and brutal crime. But what reason had the men who murdered Noakes to suppose that the law would not punish him? Every man who joined in that lawless deed has put himself on a par with Noakes. Do they realize this? We are not living here on the frontier beyond the reach of justice. There is no excuse for mob vengeance upon malefactors in California. The brutality of a crime does not afford such an excuse. Those who resort to lynching to satisfy a sentiment of indignation may think that they are justified, but they are wrong. No authority to take life is vested in the citizens, individually or collectively, save in self-defense or under the direct and explicit sanction of the law. In this case, as in all lynchings, one murder has been avenged by another. A lynching is not an execution; it is a murder. There is no sanctifying or exculatory influence about it. It is a mere reckless mob proceeding, and it is one which reflects the deepest discredit upon its participants. And we may add that next to the actual murderers in guilt and responsibility are those public journals which excuse or approve such outrages, no matter under what flimsy pretext. There is but one way to punish crime in a civilized community, and that is through the constituted machinery. All evasions of that machinery but serve to promote lawlessness, whether they are committed with criminal intent, or under the mistaken idea of furthering the ends of justice.

Tammy hall yesterday adjourned.
Tammany hall yesterday adjourned its usual celebration, and adopted resolutions of sympathy for the president.

Base ball: At Cleveland—Cleveland, 7 Providence, 4. At Albany—Albany, 8; New York, 3.

A large fire has occurred at Rovno, Russia. Five thousand families are destitute.

In Rochester, Alexander won the stallion race taking three heats out of seven-Best time 2:18.

The crops of Nebraska will be up to the average, except wheat, which will be a failure, but which never amounts to much in that state.

A fire at Biddeford, Me., destroyed the Printers' Exchange building, in Main street. The loss on the building is $20,000; insured for $9,000.

In Mount Holly, while several persons were loading a cannon, it burst, blowing a hole through the face of John Saturday and destroying his eyesight. John Woolston was also badly injured.

News is just received from Hope, Ark., of the assassination of Dock Daniels, sheriff of Columbia county, by a gang of drunken negroes on the night of July 3. He was called out of his house and shot down.

James Legrand, 79 years old, a staunch Republican, was removed from the train at Great Bend, N. Y., on Saturday so much affected by the news of President Garfield's misfortune that his physicians predicted that he would be totally insane.

In Harrisburg, Va., Wm. Banks, ten years old, the son of a colored policeman, has been committed to jail, charged with killing another negro boy, a little older than himself, by striking him upon the head with a rock and breaking his skull.

A scaffold on which five men were standing to put up a heavy piece of shafting at the Rogers locomotive works in Paterson, N. J., fell and James Parkman and George P. Berdon were fatally injured.

In Louisville, Ky., in a barroom quarrel, George Knaft was killed with a club in the hands of Mart Fig, who was himself subsequently fatally shot by E. C. Augustus. They are all young men and were employees in a brickyard in the neighborhood.

In joint convention the last Albany vote resulted as follows; Potter 27, Conkling 16, Wheeler 22, Lapham 6, Hoskins 1, Stoughton 1. Long term: Depew 32, Kernan 24, Cornell 11, Crowley 10, VanCott 1, North 1, Fisk 1, Lapham 1, Adams 1, Platt 1.

Special Correspondence of The Chicago Tribune.

Wend City, Mo., Aug. 1.—About the year 1852 a friend of mine made a pilgrimage from Henry County, Iowa, into southwest Missouri, peddling looms. He found but few settlers in the region round about Springfield and Carthage; and among the few people living there he did not find a cook-stove or match. To-day Jasper County stands fourth among the Counties of Missouri in point of population. Jasper borders on Kansas, and is two counties from the Arkansas State line. Carthage is the county-seat; and one finds there a beautiful city of 6,000 or more souls, populated by a very thriving people. For the first time in its history Jasper elected all the Republican candidates for county offices in 1880. Yet there is living a bitter feeling of resentment against the "Yankees," as evidenced by a remark I heard while on the streets of Carthage. A number of men were sitting on the outer edge of the sidewalk in front of a hotel, and as I came up even with them, one of the number—a good-looking man, aged probably 60 years—remarked that, "Before the d—d Yankees came into this country, we used to have good times." As to his meaning of good times, I think he meant pleasant times, when their enjoyment with each other was more of the camp-meeting order; for the reasons that Carthage is enjoying a healthy and enduring growth.

Three-fourths of Jasper County is reputed to be very rich in agricultural resources. I never saw finer corn growing in Iowa than is about riponing on all sides of Carthage. There are several very large flour-mills in town, and an extensive hotel is building. Four banks supply the loaning funds of the city. The southwest quarter of Jasper County is wholly given up to stony hills. Going from Iowa, where a stony farm is a curiosity, to the southwest of Jasper County, Missouri, it seemed to me, while driving over the Missouri country-roads in a buggy, that howliders as big as my head were loft right in the wagon-track on purpose for me to practice driving around. And, by the way, there's a peculiar skill requisit for a pleasant drive over those stony hills of Jasper County.

But there is a wealth yet uncomputed lying hidden under those stony hills. At a little place called Oronoco (Oro-or-no-go) lead has been worked out of the ground for some years, and it is yet a busy camp. About 1871-'2-'7 lead was discovered at Joplin, and since then an immenso amount of ore has been taken out there, aggregating millions of dollars' worth. A pretty extensive smelting-works is operating; also, as I am informed, the largest white-lead works in the country is manufacturing. Joplin has a population of 4,000, and presents a very neat appearance for a mining town, and has a number of good business-houses. The most extensive lead-lind there is worked nearly "dry," yet some shafts are drawing out vast quantities. The old mining part of the town presents a deserted appearance,—there not being a sign of a windlass, or crusher, or jig on any of the thousands of dumps scattered over a thousand acres of ground lying adjoining the north of Joplin. Each dump represents a shaft, or where one was started. The lead was, found at all depths, from ten to 100 feet. The smelting-works at Joplin have a capacity of 25,000 pounds of mineral per day.

Seven miles west of Joplin, over the line into Kansas, is another extensive find of lead, at Galena and Empire, on Short Creek.
